# Scope and prediction task

The file used is the METABRIC triple-negative (TNBC) subset: `tnbc_clinical.csv`
(30 clinical columns) joined to `tnbc_mutation.csv` (18 gene mutation flags) by
patient ID. Only this subset was available to me, so every step below
(classification, missingness, imputation, leakage audit, pipeline) is run on it.

**Prediction task.** Predict whether a patient *died of disease*
(`VITAL_STATUS = "Died of Disease"`) from information available at one
moment: **the tumour-board meeting after surgery and tumour profiling, before
adjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy or hormone therapy is decided.** Everything
in the leakage audit is judged against that moment.

```{r load}
cl <- read.csv("tnbc_clinical.csv", na.strings = c("NA", ""), check.names = FALSE,
               stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
mu <- read.csv("tnbc_mutation.csv", check.names = FALSE)
names(cl)[1] <- "PATIENT_ID"; names(mu)[1] <- "PATIENT_ID"
stopifnot(all(cl$PATIENT_ID == mu$PATIENT_ID))
genes <- setdiff(names(mu), "PATIENT_ID")
dat <- merge(cl, mu, by = "PATIENT_ID", sort = FALSE)
dat$y <- factor(ifelse(dat$VITAL_STATUS == "Died of Disease", "Died", "Living"),
                levels = c("Living", "Died"))
c(patients = nrow(dat), clinical_cols = ncol(cl), gene_cols = length(genes))
table(dat$y)
```

# 1. Classify every variable

```{r classify}
vc <- function(v, role, type, note = "") data.frame(variable = v, role = role, type = type, note = note)
classification <- rbind(
  vc("PATIENT_ID", "identifier", "nominal", "Row key, not a variable"),
  vc("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "clinical", "numeric", "Years"),
  vc("BREAST_SURGERY", "treatment", "binary", "Conserving vs mastectomy; done before the prediction moment"),
  vc("CANCER_TYPE", "clinical", "constant", "'Breast Cancer' for every patient"),
  vc("CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED", "clinical", "nominal", "Histology label, vocabulary 1"),
  vc("CELLULARITY", "clinical", "ordinal", "low < moderate < high"),
  vc("CHEMOTHERAPY", "treatment", "binary", "Adjuvant, decided after the prediction moment"),
  vc("RADIO_THERAPY", "treatment", "binary", "Adjuvant; 'YES' for every patient"),
  vc("HORMONE_THERAPY", "treatment", "binary", "Adjuvant, decided after the prediction moment"),
  vc("CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE", "genomic", "nominal", "Expression-based subtype"),
  vc("COHORT", "clinical", "nominal", "Study cohort (1-5): administrative"),
  vc("ER_IHC", "clinical", "binary", "Immunohistochemistry ER result"),
  vc("ER_STATUS", "clinical", "constant", "'-' for every patient (TNBC definition)"),
  vc("PR_STATUS", "clinical", "constant", "'-' for every patient (TNBC definition)"),
  vc("HER2_STATUS", "clinical", "constant", "'-' for every patient (TNBC definition)"),
  vc("GRADE", "clinical", "ordinal", "Tumour grade 1 < 2 < 3"),
  vc("HER2_SNP6", "genomic", "nominal", "HER2 copy-number call (GAIN/LOSS/NEUT)"),
  vc("MUTATION_COUNT", "genomic", "numeric (count)", "Number of mutations"),
  vc("HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE", "clinical", "nominal", "Histology label, vocabulary 2"),
  vc("INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE", "clinical", "binary", "pre / post"),
  vc("INTCLUST", "genomic", "nominal", "Integrative cluster (copy number + expression)"),
  vc("LATERALITY", "clinical", "binary", "Left / right"),
  vc("NPI", "clinical", "numeric", "Nottingham Prognostic Index"),
  vc("ONCOTREE_CODE", "clinical", "nominal", "Histology label, vocabulary 3"),
  vc("OS_MONTHS", "outcome", "numeric", "Overall survival time"),
  vc("SAMPLE_TYPE", "clinical", "constant", "'Primary' for every patient"),
  vc("THREEGENE", "genomic", "nominal", "Three-gene classifier from expression"),
  vc("TUMOR_SIZE", "clinical", "numeric", "mm"),
  vc("TUMOR_STAGE", "clinical", "ordinal", "0 < 1 < 2 < 3"),
  vc("VITAL_STATUS", "outcome", "binary", "The label: Died of Disease / Living"),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(genes, function(g) vc(g, "genomic", "binary", "Gene mutated (1) or not (0)")))
)
rownames(classification) <- NULL
stopifnot(setequal(classification$variable, c(names(cl), genes)))
table(classification$role)
knitr::kable(classification[classification$role != "genomic" | !classification$variable %in% genes, ])
```

The 18 mutation columns (`r paste(genes, collapse = ", ")`) are all **genomic**,
binary variables.

# 2. Missingness: by variable, and its pattern

## By variable

```{r miss-var}
miss_tab <- data.frame(variable = names(cl),
                       n_missing = sapply(cl, function(x) sum(is.na(x))))
miss_tab$pct_missing <- round(100 * miss_tab$n_missing / nrow(cl), 1)
miss_tab <- miss_tab[miss_tab$n_missing > 0, ]
miss_tab[order(-miss_tab$n_missing), ]
```

Seven variables have gaps and the remaining `r ncol(cl) - 1 - nrow(miss_tab)`
(apart from the ID) are complete. The gene mutation file has no missing values.

## Pattern

```{r miss-pattern, fig.height=5}
na_vars <- miss_tab$variable
md.pattern(cl[, na_vars], rotate.names = TRUE)
```

```{r miss-cohort}
cohort_miss <- do.call(rbind, lapply(na_vars, function(v)
  data.frame(variable = v, COHORT = sort(unique(cl$COHORT)),
             pct_missing = sapply(sort(unique(cl$COHORT)), function(k)
               100 * mean(is.na(cl[[v]][cl$COHORT == k]))))))
ggplot(cohort_miss, aes(factor(COHORT), variable, fill = pct_missing)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(pct_missing)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Percent missing, by study cohort", x = "Cohort", fill = "% missing") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r miss-tests}
p_cohort <- sapply(na_vars, function(v)
  fisher.test(table(is.na(cl[[v]]), cl$COHORT), simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 5000)$p.value)
p_outcome <- sapply(na_vars, function(v)
  fisher.test(table(is.na(cl[[v]]), dat$y))$p.value)
round(data.frame(p_missing_vs_cohort = p_cohort, p_missing_vs_outcome = p_outcome), 4)
table(THREEGENE_missing = is.na(dat$THREEGENE), dat$y)
prop.table(table(THREEGENE_missing = is.na(dat$THREEGENE), dat$y), margin = 2)
sum(is.na(cl$TUMOR_STAGE[cl$COHORT == 4])); sum(cl$COHORT == 4)
```

**Reading the pattern.**

* `TUMOR_STAGE` and `LATERALITY` are missing for essentially whole blocks of one
  cohort: all `r sum(cl$COHORT == 4)` cohort-4 patients have no stage
  (`r sum(is.na(cl$TUMOR_STAGE[cl$COHORT == 4]))` of
  `r sum(cl$COHORT == 4)`), and every missing laterality value is also in
  cohort 4. This is **structural missingness**: that cohort never recorded
  these fields. It is not random across patients, but it depends on a variable I
  can see (the cohort), so it is *missing at random given the cohort*. It is
  ignorable for imputation only if the stage-versus-other-variables
  relationship is similar in cohort 4, which I cannot check because nobody in
  that cohort has a stage.
* `THREEGENE` is missing for `r sum(is.na(dat$THREEGENE))` patients, spread over
  all cohorts. It is missing for
  `r round(100 * mean(is.na(dat$THREEGENE[dat$y == "Died"])), 1)`% of the patients who died against
  `r round(100 * mean(is.na(dat$THREEGENE[dat$y == "Living"])), 1)`% of those who lived
  (Fisher p = `r round(p_outcome["THREEGENE"], 3)`).
  `r if (p_outcome["THREEGENE"] < 0.05) "This is a statistically notable link with the outcome, so the gaps are plausibly **not** missing at random: a tumour the classifier could not call may itself be a sign of a different disease." else "The link with the outcome is not statistically significant, though the gap in rates is large enough that I treat the missingness as possibly informative."`
* `CELLULARITY`, `ER_IHC`, `GRADE` and `TUMOR_SIZE` have only a handful of
  missing values each (at most `r max(miss_tab$n_missing[miss_tab$variable %in% c("CELLULARITY", "ER_IHC", "GRADE", "TUMOR_SIZE")])`) and look like ordinary scattered gaps.

# 3. Split first, then typed imputation

## Typing every variable correctly

```{r typing}
# level labels become column names later, so make them unique, plain ASCII names
# ("4ER-" and "4ER+" would otherwise both turn into "4ER.")
clean_lv <- function(f, signs = FALSE) {
  lv <- levels(f)
  if (signs) lv <- gsub("-", "neg", gsub("\\+", "pos", lv))
  levels(f) <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9]+", "_", lv)
  f
}
typed <- function(d) {
  out <- data.frame(
    AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS = as.numeric(d$AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS),
    NPI = as.numeric(d$NPI),
    TUMOR_SIZE = as.numeric(d$TUMOR_SIZE),
    MUTATION_COUNT = as.numeric(d$MUTATION_COUNT),
    GRADE = factor(ifelse(is.na(d$GRADE), NA, ifelse(d$GRADE == 3, "3", "1-2")),
                   levels = c("1-2", "3"), ordered = TRUE),
    TUMOR_STAGE = factor(ifelse(is.na(d$TUMOR_STAGE), NA,
                                ifelse(d$TUMOR_STAGE <= 1, "0-1", as.character(d$TUMOR_STAGE))),
                         levels = c("0-1", "2", "3"), ordered = TRUE),
    CELLULARITY = factor(d$CELLULARITY, levels = c("low", "moderate", "high"), ordered = TRUE),
    ER_IHC = factor(d$ER_IHC), LATERALITY = factor(d$LATERALITY),
    BREAST_SURGERY = factor(d$BREAST_SURGERY),
    INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE = factor(d$INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE),
    CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE = factor(d$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE), HER2_SNP6 = factor(d$HER2_SNP6),
    INTCLUST = factor(d$INTCLUST), THREEGENE = factor(d$THREEGENE),
    COHORT = factor(d$COHORT))
  out$INTCLUST  <- clean_lv(out$INTCLUST, signs = TRUE)
  out$THREEGENE <- clean_lv(out$THREEGENE, signs = TRUE)
  out$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE <- clean_lv(out$CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE)
  out$BREAST_SURGERY  <- clean_lv(out$BREAST_SURGERY)
  out
}
numeric_v <- c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT")
ordinal_v <- c("GRADE", "TUMOR_STAGE", "CELLULARITY")
nominal_v <- c("BREAST_SURGERY", "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE", "LATERALITY", "ER_IHC",
               "CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE", "HER2_SNP6", "INTCLUST", "THREEGENE")
X <- typed(dat)
sapply(X, function(x) class(x)[1])
table(dat$GRADE, useNA = "ifany"); table(dat$TUMOR_STAGE, useNA = "ifany")
```

Grade 1 has 2 patients and stage 0 has 1 patient, too few for any model to
learn, so I merged them into the next level (grade `1-2`, stage `0-1`). The
ordering is kept, so both stay *ordered* factors, not numbers.

## Split first

```{r split}
set.seed(2026)
s  <- sample.split(dat$y, SplitRatio = 0.7)      # stratified on the outcome
tr <- which(s); te <- which(!s)
rbind(train = table(dat$y[tr]), test = table(dat$y[te]))
```

From here on, **nothing is learned from the test rows**: not an imputation
model, not a mean, not a selected feature.

## Which imputer is better? A masking experiment on the training rows

To compare methods I hide 25% of the *known* stages in the training rows,
impute them, and score the guesses against the truth.

```{r mask-exp, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(7)
known <- which(!is.na(X$TUMOR_STAGE[tr]) & X$COHORT[tr] != "4")
base  <- X[tr, ]
lv    <- levels(base$TUMOR_STAGE)
score <- function(truth, guess_num) {
  g <- pmin(pmax(round(guess_num), 1), 3)
  c(acc = mean(g == as.integer(truth)), mae = mean(abs(guess_num - as.integer(truth))),
    nonint = mean(abs(guess_num - round(guess_num)) > 1e-9))
}
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, function(i) {
  hide <- sample(known, round(0.25 * length(known)))
  d <- base; truth <- d$TUMOR_STAGE[hide]; d$TUMOR_STAGE[hide] <- NA
  mk <- function(method, dd) {
    mt <- make.method(dd); mt[] <- ""
    mt[colSums(is.na(dd)) > 0] <- "pmm"; mt["TUMOR_STAGE"] <- method
    for (v in c("GRADE", "CELLULARITY")) if (any(is.na(dd[[v]]))) mt[v] <- "polr"
    for (v in c("ER_IHC", "LATERALITY")) if (any(is.na(dd[[v]]))) mt[v] <- "logreg"
    if (any(is.na(dd$THREEGENE))) mt["THREEGENE"] <- "cart"
    # mice's polr/logreg fail when a variable has exactly one gap: use a tree there
    one <- names(mt)[colSums(is.na(dd)) == 1 & !names(mt) %in% c("TUMOR_STAGE", numeric_v)]
    mt[one] <- "cart"
    mt[colSums(is.na(dd)) == 0] <- ""
    mt
  }
  # (a) treated as continuous
  dn <- d; dn$TUMOR_STAGE <- as.numeric(dn$TUMOR_STAGE)
  gn <- suppressWarnings(mice::complete(mice(dn, m = 1, maxit = 5, method = mk("norm", dn),
                                       printFlag = FALSE, seed = i), 1))$TUMOR_STAGE[hide]
  # (b) ordered factor with proportional odds
  go <- suppressWarnings(mice::complete(mice(d, m = 1, maxit = 5, method = mk("polr", d),
                                       printFlag = FALSE, seed = i), 1))$TUMOR_STAGE[hide]
  # (b2) random-forest imputation inside mice (still typed: it sees an ordered factor)
  gr <- suppressWarnings(mice::complete(mice(d, m = 1, maxit = 5, method = mk("rf", d), ntrees = 100,
                                       printFlag = FALSE, seed = i), 1))$TUMOR_STAGE[hide]
  # (c) missForest
  gf <- suppressWarnings(missForest(d, ntree = 100, verbose = FALSE)$ximp)$TUMOR_STAGE[hide]
  # (d) mode
  md <- names(which.max(table(d$TUMOR_STAGE)))
  rbind(data.frame(method = "treated as continuous (norm)", t(score(truth, gn))),
        data.frame(method = "mice polr (ordered factor)", t(score(truth, as.integer(go)))),
        data.frame(method = "mice rf (random forest)", t(score(truth, as.integer(gr)))),
        data.frame(method = "missForest", t(score(truth, as.integer(gf)))),
        data.frame(method = "most common level", t(score(truth, rep(match(md, lv), length(hide))))))
}))
mask_summary <- aggregate(cbind(acc, mae, nonint) ~ method, data = res, FUN = mean)
mask_summary[, -1] <- round(mask_summary[, -1], 3)
names(mask_summary) <- c("method", "exact_match", "mean_abs_error_in_stages", "share_non_integer")
mask_summary[order(-mask_summary$exact_match), ]

# pick the best method that can be fitted on training rows only and applied to new rows
em <- setNames(mask_summary$exact_match, mask_summary$method)
stage_method <- if (em["mice rf (random forest)"] > em["mice polr (ordered factor)"]) "rf" else "polr"
stage_method
```

`missForest` scored highest, but it has no way to fill new rows from a model it
learned (the test rows would have to take part in fitting it), so it cannot be
used in a split-first pipeline. Among methods that **can** be fitted on the
training rows and applied to the test rows (`mice` with the `ignore` argument),
the best for `TUMOR_STAGE` is **`mice` with `r stage_method`**
(`r round(100 * em[ifelse(stage_method == "rf", "mice rf (random forest)", "mice polr (ordered factor)")])`% exact match, against
`r round(100 * em["most common level"])`% for always guessing the most common stage).
I use that for `TUMOR_STAGE`, and keep `polr` for the other ordered variables,
which have only a handful of gaps and are too few to test the same way.

## Typed imputation with mice, learned on the training rows only

Each variable with gaps gets the method that matches its type. `mice`'s
`ignore` argument keeps the test rows out of every model fit while still
filling their gaps from models trained on the training rows.

```{r mice-run}
st   <- rbind(X[tr, ], X[te, ])
ign  <- c(rep(FALSE, length(tr)), rep(TRUE, length(te)))
meth <- make.method(st); meth[] <- ""
meth[numeric_v]                     <- "pmm"      # numeric: predictive mean matching
meth[c("GRADE", "CELLULARITY")]     <- "polr"    # ordered factor: proportional odds
meth["TUMOR_STAGE"]                 <- stage_method  # chosen by the masking experiment above
meth[c("ER_IHC", "LATERALITY")]     <- "logreg"   # two-level factor: logistic regression
meth["THREEGENE"]                   <- "cart"     # sparse 4-level factor: classification tree
meth[colSums(is.na(st)) == 0]       <- ""         # nothing to impute
meth[meth != ""]

imp <- suppressWarnings(mice(st, m = 5, maxit = 10, method = meth, ntrees = 100,
                             predictorMatrix = make.predictorMatrix(st),
                             ignore = ign, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE))
Xc <- mice::complete(imp, 1)
c(remaining_NA = sum(is.na(Xc)))
Xc_tr <- Xc[seq_along(tr), ]; Xc_te <- Xc[-seq_along(tr), ]
```

**How stable are the imputed values?** With five imputations, this is the share
of missing cells where all five draws agree.

```{r stability-imp}
agree <- sapply(names(meth[meth != ""]), function(v) {
  m <- imp$imp[[v]]
  if (is.null(m) || nrow(m) == 0) return(NA)
  mean(apply(m, 1, function(r) length(unique(r)) == 1))
})
data.frame(variable = names(agree), method = meth[names(agree)],
           n_imputed = sapply(names(agree), function(v) nrow(imp$imp[[v]])),
           pct_all_five_agree = round(100 * agree))
```

One warning about `TUMOR_STAGE`: because every cohort-4 patient is missing
stage, the observed stages carry no information about how cohort 4 differs
(the cohort is not a usable predictor for it). Those patients' stage is
predicted from their other variables only, and my masking experiment (which hid
stages only in the other cohorts) cannot show how well that works for cohort 4.

# 4. Leakage audit

The question for each candidate: **would this value be known, and would it be
unaffected by the outcome, at the tumour-board moment defined above?**

```{r leakage-table}
audit <- data.frame(
  variable = c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "BREAST_SURGERY", "CELLULARITY", "GRADE",
               "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE", "LATERALITY", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "TUMOR_STAGE",
               "ER_IHC", "CLAUDIN_SUBTYPE", "HER2_SNP6", "MUTATION_COUNT", "INTCLUST",
               "THREEGENE", "18 gene mutation flags", "COHORT",
               "OS_MONTHS", "VITAL_STATUS", "CHEMOTHERAPY", "HORMONE_THERAPY", "RADIO_THERAPY"),
  known_when = c("At diagnosis", "At surgery", "Pathology after surgery", "Pathology after surgery",
                 "At diagnosis", "At diagnosis", "Pathology (size, grade, nodes)",
                 "Pathology after surgery", "Pathology after surgery", "Pathology after surgery",
                 "Tumour expression profiling", "Tumour copy-number profiling",
                 "Tumour sequencing", "Tumour copy-number and expression profiling",
                 "Tumour expression profiling", "Tumour sequencing",
                 "Which study the patient joined",
                 "Years of follow-up after the decision", "End of follow-up",
                 "After the board decides", "After the board decides", "After the board decides"),
  known_at_moment = c(rep("yes", 17), "no", "no (it is the label)", "no", "no", "no"),
  verdict = c(rep("keep", 16), "keep as imputation helper only, not a predictor",
              "remove: leakage", "label", "remove: leakage", "remove: leakage", "remove: leakage"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(audit)
```

Notes on the judgement calls:

* **Genomic variables** are legitimate only if tumour profiling has been done
  before the decision. I assume it has (it is also what next week's TNBC model
  needs), but it would not be true for a clinic without sequencing.
* **`NPI`** is derived from size, grade and nodal status, so it is known after
  pathology, but it largely repeats `TUMOR_SIZE` and `GRADE`; the correlation
  step below deals with that, not leakage.
* **`COHORT`** is known at the time but is a study artefact (site and period),
  not biology; I use it only to help imputation, never as a predictor.
* **Treatment** variables record decisions made *after* the moment: a model
  using them would be reading the board's own view of the prognosis.

## A statistical filter would pick the leaky variables

This is the check that shows why leakage is a separate problem from statistical
selection. Information gain (in bits) on the training rows, for the leaky
variables and for the best legitimate ones:

```{r leak-ig}
H <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 0]; -sum(p * log2(p)) }
ig1 <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.numeric(x) && length(unique(x)) > 2) {
    br <- unique(quantile(x, 0:4 / 4, na.rm = TRUE))
    x <- cut(x, br, include.lowest = TRUE)
  }
  tab <- table(x, y); px <- rowSums(tab) / sum(tab)
  H(prop.table(table(y))) - sum(px * apply(tab, 1, function(r) H(r / sum(r))))
}
ytr <- dat$y[tr]
leaky <- data.frame(OS_MONTHS = dat$OS_MONTHS, CHEMOTHERAPY = dat$CHEMOTHERAPY,
                    HORMONE_THERAPY = dat$HORMONE_THERAPY)[tr, ]
legit <- cbind(Xc_tr[, c("NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "GRADE", "TUMOR_STAGE", "AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS")],
               dat[tr, c("TP53", "PIK3CA")])
ig_compare <- c(sapply(leaky, ig1, y = ytr), sapply(as.data.frame(lapply(legit, function(z) if (is.ordered(z)) as.integer(z) else z)), ig1, y = ytr))
data.frame(variable = names(ig_compare), info_gain_bits = round(ig_compare, 3),
           type = c(rep("leaky", ncol(leaky)), rep("legitimate", ncol(legit))))[order(-ig_compare), ]
```

`OS_MONTHS` carries far more information about the outcome than any legitimate
predictor, because survival time and vital status are two sides of the same
event. It would be selected first by any data-driven filter, which is why it has
to be removed by *reasoning*, before the statistics.

# 5. TNBC feature pipeline (learned on the training rows only)

Candidate predictors after the domain and leakage decisions: 10 clinical, 5
genomic summary variables and 18 gene flags. The test rows get the *same*
transformations, never refitted.

## Encoding

* Numeric variables stay numeric.
* Ordered factors become integer codes that respect the order.
* Nominal factors become one-hot columns (`fullRank`, so one level is the baseline).
* Gene flags are already 0/1.

```{r encode}
make_feat <- function(Xcomp, rows) {
  f <- Xcomp[, c(numeric_v, ordinal_v, nominal_v)]
  for (o in ordinal_v) f[[o]] <- as.integer(f[[o]])
  cbind(f, dat[rows, genes])
}
feat_tr <- make_feat(Xc_tr, tr); feat_te <- make_feat(Xc_te, te)
dv  <- dummyVars(~ ., data = feat_tr, fullRank = TRUE)
Etr <- predict(dv, feat_tr); Ete <- predict(dv, feat_te)
colnames(Etr) <- colnames(Ete) <- make.names(colnames(Etr), unique = TRUE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(colnames(Etr)))
c(encoded_columns = ncol(Etr), train_rows = nrow(Etr), test_rows = nrow(Ete))
all_vars <- c(numeric_v, ordinal_v, nominal_v, genes)
map_var <- function(cols) sapply(cols, function(cn) {
  hit <- all_vars[startsWith(cn, all_vars)]
  hit[which.max(nchar(hit))]
})
col_var <- map_var(colnames(Etr))
```

## Step 1: near-zero variance, then scaling

```{r nzv}
nz <- nearZeroVar(Etr, saveMetrics = TRUE)
keep_nzv <- rownames(nz)[!nz$nzv]
Etr1 <- Etr[, keep_nzv]; Ete1 <- Ete[, keep_nzv]
c(before = ncol(Etr), after_nzv = ncol(Etr1))
# scaling parameters come from the TRAINING rows only
pp  <- preProcess(Etr1, method = c("center", "scale"))
Str <- predict(pp, Etr1); Ste <- predict(pp, Ete1)
round(c(train_mean_NPI = mean(Str[, "NPI"]), test_mean_NPI = mean(Ste[, "NPI"]),
        train_sd_NPI = sd(Str[, "NPI"]), test_sd_NPI = sd(Ste[, "NPI"])), 3)
```

Columns with near-zero variance (here, mostly rare mutations) are dropped. The
test set is *not* exactly mean 0, SD 1: that is correct, it was scaled with the
training numbers.

## Step 2: correlation

```{r corr}
cm <- cor(Str)
pairs <- which(upper.tri(cm), arr.ind = TRUE)
top <- data.frame(a = colnames(cm)[pairs[, 1]], b = colnames(cm)[pairs[, 2]], r = cm[pairs])
top <- top[order(-abs(top$r)), ]
head(top, 8)
# Tie-break by domain knowledge: menopausal state is *inferred from age*, so when the
# two are highly correlated I drop the derived variable and keep age (the richer one).
drop_derived <- if (abs(cm["AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE.pre"]) > 0.8)
  "INFERRED_MENOPAUSAL_STATE.pre" else character(0)
rest <- setdiff(colnames(cm), drop_derived)
corr_drop <- c(drop_derived, findCorrelation(cm[rest, rest], cutoff = 0.8, names = TRUE))
corr_drop
keep_corr <- setdiff(colnames(Str), corr_drop)
```

```{r corr-plot, fig.height=6}
cm_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cm)); names(cm_long) <- c("a", "b", "r")
top_cols <- unique(c(head(top$a, 6), head(top$b, 6), "NPI", "TUMOR_STAGE", "GRADE", "TUMOR_SIZE"))
top_cols <- intersect(top_cols, colnames(cm))
ggplot(subset(cm_long, a %in% top_cols & b %in% top_cols), aes(a, b, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() + geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation among the most related features (training rows)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Step 3: information gain (with a permutation null)

For each remaining column I compute the information gain about the outcome (in
bits, numeric columns cut into quartiles) and compare it with the gain I would
get from the same column if the outcome labels were shuffled. A column is kept
only if its real gain exceeds the 95th percentile of its own shuffled gains.

```{r ig, cache=TRUE}
ig_vec <- function(M, y) sapply(seq_len(ncol(M)), function(j) ig1(M[, j], y))
set.seed(11)
M <- Etr1[, keep_corr, drop = FALSE]
ig_real <- ig_vec(M, ytr)
null <- replicate(300, ig_vec(M, sample(ytr)))
ig_thr <- apply(null, 1, quantile, probs = 0.95)
ig_tab <- data.frame(column = colnames(M), variable = col_var[colnames(M)],
                     info_gain = ig_real, null_95 = ig_thr, keep = ig_real > ig_thr)
ig_tab <- ig_tab[order(-ig_tab$info_gain), ]
rownames(ig_tab) <- NULL
ig_keep <- ig_tab$column[ig_tab$keep]
head(ig_tab, 12)
c(tested = nrow(ig_tab), kept = length(ig_keep))
```

## Step 4: recursive feature elimination (RFE)

```{r rfe, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(13)
xr <- as.data.frame(Str[, ig_keep, drop = FALSE])
sizes <- sort(unique(pmin(c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20), ncol(xr))))
ctrl <- rfeControl(functions = rfFuncs, method = "repeatedcv", number = 5, repeats = 3)
rfe_fit <- rfe(x = xr, y = ytr, sizes = sizes, rfeControl = ctrl, ntree = 300)
rfe_sel <- predictors(rfe_fit)
rfe_fit$results[, c("Variables", "Accuracy", "Kappa")]
rfe_sel
```

```{r rfe-plot, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(rfe_fit$results, aes(Variables, Accuracy)) + geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = length(rfe_sel), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "RFE: cross-validated accuracy by number of features (training rows)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

RFE picks the smallest subset whose cross-validated accuracy is within 1.5% of
the best, which gives **`r length(rfe_sel)` features**.

```{r sanity}
auc <- function(score, y) {
  r <- rank(score); n1 <- sum(y == "Died"); n0 <- sum(y == "Living")
  (sum(r[y == "Died"]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
yte <- dat$y[te]
set.seed(5)
rf_all <- randomForest(x = as.data.frame(Str[, keep_nzv]), y = ytr, ntree = 500)
rf_sel <- randomForest(x = as.data.frame(Str[, rfe_sel, drop = FALSE]), y = ytr, ntree = 500)
data.frame(features = c(ncol(Str), length(rfe_sel)),
           test_AUC = round(c(auc(predict(rf_all, as.data.frame(Ste), type = "prob")[, "Died"], yte),
                              auc(predict(rf_sel, as.data.frame(Ste[, rfe_sel, drop = FALSE]), type = "prob")[, "Died"], yte)), 3),
           row.names = c("all columns after near-zero-variance filter", "RFE-selected"))
```

This is only a sanity check that the pipeline runs end to end on held-out rows
(the test set has only `r length(te)` patients, so differences of a few points
mean nothing); the four-model comparison is next week's job.

## Step 5: principal components

PCA is fitted on the **scaled training** features after the correlation filter,
and the test rows are projected with the same rotation.

```{r pca}
pca <- prcomp(Str[, keep_corr], center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
ve <- summary(pca)$importance
round(ve[, 1:6], 3)
pcs_te <- predict(pca, Ste[, keep_corr])
load_top <- function(k, n = 8) {
  l <- pca$rotation[, k]; l[order(-abs(l))][1:n]
}
round(load_top(1), 3)
round(load_top(2), 3)
```

```{r pca-plot, fig.height=4.5}
sc <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2], outcome = ytr)
ggplot(sc, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = outcome)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_ellipse() +
  labs(title = paste0("Training rows in PC space (PC1 ", round(100 * ve[2, 1], 1),
                      "%, PC2 ", round(100 * ve[2, 2], 1), "% of variance)")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r pca-leak}
# How much would the rotation change if PCA had been fitted on ALL rows (the leak)?
S_all <- rbind(Str[, keep_corr], Ste[, keep_corr])
pca_all <- prcomp(S_all, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)
cos1 <- abs(sum(pca$rotation[, 1] * pca_all$rotation[, 1]))
cos2 <- abs(sum(pca$rotation[, 2] * pca_all$rotation[, 2]))
c(cosine_PC1_train_vs_all = round(cos1, 4), cosine_PC2_train_vs_all = round(cos2, 4),
  test_rows_PC1_mean_trainfit = round(mean(pcs_te[, 1]), 3),
  test_rows_PC1_mean_allfit = round(mean(predict(pca_all, Ste[, keep_corr])[, 1]), 3))
```

# 6. Table of removed variables

One row per removed variable: its reason (**domain exclusion**, **leakage
prevention** or **statistical selection**) and a sentence of justification. The
statistical sentences are generated from the numbers above.

```{r removed}
# ---- statistical selection: stage at which each variable's LAST column is removed
col_stage <- rep("kept", ncol(Etr)); names(col_stage) <- colnames(Etr)
col_stage[!colnames(Etr) %in% keep_nzv] <- "nzv"
col_stage[colnames(Etr) %in% corr_drop] <- "correlation"
col_stage[colnames(Etr) %in% setdiff(keep_corr, ig_keep)] <- "info_gain"
col_stage[colnames(Etr) %in% setdiff(ig_keep, rfe_sel)] <- "rfe"
order_st <- c(nzv = 1, correlation = 2, info_gain = 3, rfe = 4)

stat_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(unique(col_var), function(v) {
  cols <- names(col_var)[col_var == v]
  st <- col_stage[cols]
  if (any(st == "kept")) return(NULL)               # at least one column survives
  last <- names(which.max(order_st[st]))
  cl_last <- cols[st == last]
  sentence <- switch(last,
    nzv = {
      if (v %in% genes) sprintf("Mutated in only %d of %d training patients (%.1f%%), too few events to learn from.",
                                sum(feat_tr[[v]]), nrow(feat_tr), 100 * mean(feat_tr[[v]]))
      else sprintf("One value covers %.0f%% of the training patients, so it adds almost no information.",
                   100 * max(prop.table(table(feat_tr[[v]]))))
    },
    correlation = {
      cc <- cl_last[1]
      others <- setdiff(keep_corr, cc)
      rr <- cm[cc, others]; nm <- names(which.max(abs(rr)))
      sprintf("Correlated r = %.2f with %s, so it repeats information that variable already carries.", rr[nm], nm)
    },
    info_gain = {
      ii <- ig_tab[ig_tab$column %in% cl_last, ]
      sprintf("Information gain %.4f bits, not above the %.4f bits it reaches with shuffled outcomes, so no real signal.",
              max(ii$info_gain), ii$null_95[which.max(ii$info_gain)])
    },
    rfe = sprintf("Dropped by RFE: the best %d-feature subset scored within 1.5%% of the top cross-validated accuracy without it.", length(rfe_sel)))
  data.frame(variable = v, reason = "statistical selection",
             justification = sprintf("%s (stage: %s)", sentence,
                                     c(nzv = "near-zero variance", correlation = "correlation filter",
                                       info_gain = "information gain", rfe = "RFE")[last]))
}))

# ---- domain exclusions and leakage prevention (decided before looking at the data)
dom <- data.frame(
  variable = c("PATIENT_ID", "CANCER_TYPE", "SAMPLE_TYPE", "ER_STATUS", "PR_STATUS", "HER2_STATUS",
               "CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED", "HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE", "ONCOTREE_CODE", "COHORT"),
  reason = "domain exclusion",
  justification = c(
    "A row identifier carries no biology and would let a model memorise patients.",
    "Every patient has 'Breast Cancer', so it cannot separate anyone.",
    "Every patient has a 'Primary' sample, so it cannot separate anyone.",
    "'-' for all 190 patients because TNBC is defined by negative ER, so it is constant by construction.",
    "'-' for all 190 patients because TNBC is defined by negative PR, so it is constant by construction.",
    "'-' for all 190 patients because TNBC is defined by negative HER2, so it is constant by construction.",
    "One of three overlapping histology vocabularies for the same tumours; the labels also differ by cohort coding.",
    "A second histology vocabulary overlapping the other two; kept out to avoid triple-counting one fact.",
    "A third histology vocabulary overlapping the other two; kept out to avoid triple-counting one fact.",
    "Study site and period, not biology; a model could learn 'which cohort' as a shortcut for follow-up length. Used only to help imputation."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
leak <- data.frame(
  variable = c("OS_MONTHS", "VITAL_STATUS", "CHEMOTHERAPY", "HORMONE_THERAPY", "RADIO_THERAPY"),
  reason = "leakage prevention",
  justification = c(
    "Survival time is the outcome measured another way, and it has far more information gain than any legitimate predictor.",
    "This is the label itself.",
    "Decided after the prediction moment, and chosen by clinicians who already judge prognosis.",
    "Decided after the prediction moment, and chosen by clinicians who already judge prognosis.",
    "Decided after the prediction moment (and 'YES' for every patient here, so also constant)."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

removed <- rbind(dom, leak, stat_rows)
rownames(removed) <- NULL
removed <- removed[order(factor(removed$reason, levels = c("domain exclusion", "leakage prevention", "statistical selection"))), ]
rownames(removed) <- NULL
table(removed$reason)
knitr::kable(removed)
```

```{r kept}
kept_vars <- setdiff(all_vars, removed$variable)
```

**Kept after the whole pipeline:** `r length(kept_vars)` of the
`r length(all_vars)` candidate variables have at least one column in the final
RFE subset (`r paste(kept_vars, collapse = ", ")`); the selected columns are
`r paste(rfe_sel, collapse = ", ")`. The other
`r length(all_vars) - length(kept_vars)` candidates appear in the table above, and
`r sum(removed$reason != "statistical selection")` more variables were excluded
before the pipeline by the domain and leakage decisions.

# Is imputing before the split really worse? An experiment

I repeat the whole pipeline on 25 different random 70/30 splits and compare the
held-out AUC of a random forest in three set-ups:

* **A (correct):** split first; impute and select features using the training rows only.
* **B (impute first):** impute using all 190 rows *with the outcome in the imputation model*, then split.
* **C (select first):** split, impute correctly, but choose the top-8 features by information gain using *all* rows, test rows included.

```{r leak-exp, cache=TRUE}
enc_simple <- function(Xcomp, rows) {
  f <- Xcomp[, c(numeric_v, ordinal_v, nominal_v)]
  for (o in ordinal_v) f[[o]] <- as.integer(f[[o]])
  M <- model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = f)
  M <- cbind(M, as.matrix(dat[rows, genes]))
  colnames(M) <- make.names(colnames(M)); M
}
ig_cols <- function(M, y) sapply(seq_len(ncol(M)), function(j) ig1(M[, j], y))
mice_fit <- function(stk, ignore = NULL) {
  mt <- make.method(stk); mt[] <- ""
  mt[intersect(numeric_v, names(mt))] <- "pmm"
  mt[c("GRADE", "CELLULARITY")] <- "polr"; mt["TUMOR_STAGE"] <- stage_method
  mt[c("ER_IHC", "LATERALITY")] <- "logreg"; mt["THREEGENE"] <- "cart"
  one <- names(mt)[colSums(is.na(stk)) == 1 & !names(mt) %in% numeric_v]
  mt[one] <- "cart"
  mt[colSums(is.na(stk)) == 0] <- ""
  suppressWarnings(mice::complete(mice(stk, m = 1, maxit = 3, method = mt, ignore = ignore,
                                       ntrees = 50, printFlag = FALSE, seed = 1), 1))
}
run_rep <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  s <- sample.split(dat$y, SplitRatio = 0.7); tr <- which(s); te <- which(!s)
  ytr <- dat$y[tr]; yte <- dat$y[te]
  # A and C: impute with training rows only (outcome NOT in the model)
  stk <- rbind(X[tr, ], X[te, ]); ig <- c(rep(FALSE, length(tr)), rep(TRUE, length(te)))
  C1 <- mice_fit(stk, ig)
  Mtr <- enc_simple(C1[seq_along(tr), ], tr); Mte <- enc_simple(C1[-seq_along(tr), ], te)
  # A: select on train
  selA <- order(-ig_cols(Mtr, ytr))[1:8]
  # C: select on all rows
  Mall <- rbind(Mtr, Mte); yall <- factor(c(as.character(ytr), as.character(yte)), levels = levels(ytr))
  selC <- order(-ig_cols(Mall, yall))[1:8]
  # B: impute on all rows with the outcome as a predictor, then split
  XB <- X; XB$y <- dat$y
  CB <- mice_fit(XB)
  MB <- enc_simple(CB[, setdiff(names(CB), "y")], seq_len(nrow(dat)))
  selB <- order(-ig_cols(MB[tr, ], ytr))[1:8]
  fit_auc <- function(Mtrain, Mtest, sel) {
    rf <- randomForest(x = Mtrain[, sel], y = ytr, ntree = 300)
    auc(predict(rf, Mtest[, sel], type = "prob")[, "Died"], yte)
  }
  c(A = fit_auc(Mtr, Mte, selA), B = fit_auc(MB[tr, ], MB[te, ], selB), C = fit_auc(Mtr, Mte, selC))
}
reps <- t(sapply(1:25, run_rep))
leak_summary <- data.frame(
  setup = c("A: correct", "B: impute first", "C: select first"),
  mean_test_AUC = round(colMeans(reps), 4),
  diff_vs_A = round(colMeans(reps) - mean(reps[, "A"]), 4),
  se_of_diff = round(c(0, sd(reps[, "B"] - reps[, "A"]), sd(reps[, "C"] - reps[, "A"])) / sqrt(nrow(reps)), 4))
leak_summary
```

```{r scale-leak}
# magnitude of the simplest leak: scaling parameters from all rows vs from training rows
sl <- data.frame(
  variable = c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT"),
  mean_train = sapply(c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT"), function(v) mean(Xc_tr[[v]])),
  mean_all = sapply(c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT"), function(v) mean(Xc[[v]])),
  sd_train = sapply(c("AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "MUTATION_COUNT"), function(v) sd(Xc_tr[[v]])))
sl$mean_shift_in_SDs <- round((sl$mean_all - sl$mean_train) / sl$sd_train, 3)
sl[, c("variable", "mean_shift_in_SDs")]
```

# Written answers

## 1. Three reasons for removing a variable

```{r example-pick, include=FALSE}
ex <- stat_rows[stat_rows$variable == "MEN1", ]
if (nrow(ex) == 0) ex <- stat_rows[1, ]
ex_var <- ex$variable[1]; ex_just <- ex$justification[1]
```

* **Domain exclusion:** `ER_STATUS` (and `PR_STATUS`, `HER2_STATUS`) is `-` for
  every one of the `r nrow(dat)` patients, because triple-negative disease is
  *defined* by negative ER, PR and HER2. No data analysis is needed to know that
  a constant cannot predict anything, and nobody could build a predictor on it.
* **Leakage prevention:** `OS_MONTHS`. It has an information gain of
  `r round(ig_compare["OS_MONTHS"], 2)` bits about death from disease against
  `r round(max(ig_compare[c("NPI", "TUMOR_SIZE", "GRADE", "TUMOR_STAGE", "AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS", "TP53", "PIK3CA")]), 2)` bits
  for the best legitimate variable I checked, because survival time and vital
  status describe the same event. It is not known at the tumour board.
* **Statistical selection:** for example `r ex_var`:
  `r ex_just`

**Why three reasons, not one.** They are different kinds of decision, with
different evidence and different failure modes. Domain exclusion is knowledge
about what a column *is*, so it is made before looking at outcomes and cannot
be tuned. Leakage prevention is about **time and causality**: the offending
variable is the one the statistics like best (`OS_MONTHS` tops the information
gain table), so a data-driven filter would keep it and only reasoning removes
it. Statistical selection is the only one that depends on the sample, so it is
the only one that must be *re-learned inside the training rows*, otherwise it
leaks too (see the experiment). Merging them into one "feature selection" step
would let a statistical rule do the job of a clinical judgement, which it
cannot.

## 2. Why imputation must be learned after the split

An imputation model (a mean, a regression, a forest) is a fitted model like any
other. If I fit it on all 190 rows, the values filled into the *test* rows are
computed from training **and test** information, and when the outcome is in the
imputation model, partly from the test patients' own outcomes. The test set then
stops being unseen data, so the held-out score is too good.

What goes wrong, concretely: a missing stage in a test patient is filled using a
model that has seen that patient's neighbours' labels and that patient's own
outcome, which can make a test case look easier than a new patient will be at
the bedside.

**How large is the error here?** I expected it to be small for imputation and
larger for anything that chooses things using the outcome. Measured over 25
random splits, held-out AUC was `r leak_summary$mean_test_AUC[1]` with the
correct pipeline, `r leak_summary$mean_test_AUC[2]` when I imputed first
(difference `r leak_summary$diff_vs_A[2]`, standard error
`r leak_summary$se_of_diff[2]`) and `r leak_summary$mean_test_AUC[3]` when I
selected features on all rows (difference `r leak_summary$diff_vs_A[3]`,
standard error `r leak_summary$se_of_diff[3]`).

* `r if (abs(leak_summary$diff_vs_A[2]) < 2 * leak_summary$se_of_diff[2]) "**Imputation:** the leak is within noise here. Only a few percent of the cells are missing, so there is little for it to leak into, and the standardising leak moves the means by at most " else "**Imputation:** the leak is large enough to see here, and the standardising leak moves the means by at most "` `r max(abs(sl$mean_shift_in_SDs))` standard deviations.
* **Feature selection:** this is the leak that matters here. Choosing the
  top-8 features with all rows inflated the AUC by about
  `r leak_summary$diff_vs_A[3]`, roughly `r round(leak_summary$diff_vs_A[3] / leak_summary$se_of_diff[3])` standard errors, and an
  inflation of that size is bigger than the differences between models I would
  be trying to detect next week. It grows with the number of candidate features
  (here 33 for 133 training rows).

So the penalty for imputing first is small *in this dataset*, but I cannot know
that in advance, the correct order costs nothing, and for selection the
penalty is real.

## 3. Imputing tumour grade (or stage) as if continuous

Grade and stage are **ordered categories**, not measurements. The distance from
grade 1 to grade 2 is not the same kind of quantity as from 2 to 3, and "grade
2.4" is not a grade. A continuous imputer fills gaps with values like 2.4
or 1.8; in my masking experiment `r round(100 * mask_summary$share_non_integer[mask_summary$method == "treated as continuous (norm)"])`% of the guessed stages were not whole numbers, and rounding them back
gave an exact match rate of only
`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "treated as continuous (norm)"])`%,
**worse than always guessing the most common stage**
(`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "most common level"])`%). Treating the ordered stage as a category
did better: `r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "mice rf (random forest)"])`% with `mice` random forests,
`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "mice polr (ordered factor)"])`% with `mice` proportional-odds (`polr`) and
`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "missForest"])`% with `missForest`. The `polr` result is not impressive: with
only about a hundred observed stages and many predictors, a proportional-odds
model does *worse* than guessing the mode
(`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "mice polr (ordered factor)"])`% against
`r round(100 * mask_summary$exact_match[mask_summary$method == "most common level"])`%), which is why I did not use it for stage. (Grade is the same kind of variable; stage is the one with enough gaps to
test.)

* **mice** fills each variable from its own model chosen for the variable's
  type (here: predictive mean matching, proportional-odds regression, logistic
  regression, classification trees) and draws from a predictive distribution,
  so it gives *several* completed datasets and expresses imputation
  uncertainty. It assumes data are **missing at random** given the variables in
  the model, and that each of those conditional models is reasonable.
* **missForest** fits a random forest for each variable and iterates. It
  assumes missing at random too, but makes **no** distributional or linearity
  assumption, so it copes with interactions and mixed types, at the price of
  giving one imputed value per gap (no uncertainty) and no way to fill new rows
  from a stored model.

**My choices:** `pmm` for the numeric variable with gaps (`TUMOR_SIZE`; it only
returns observed values, so no impossible sizes); `rf` inside `mice` for
`TUMOR_STAGE` (ordered, 46 gaps, the best method I could test that fits the
split-first rule); `polr` for `GRADE` and `CELLULARITY` (ordered, only 2 and 6
gaps, too few to test); `logreg` for `ER_IHC` and `LATERALITY` (two levels);
`cart` for `THREEGENE` (sparse, four levels, where a regression is unstable).
`missForest` scored higher on stage, but I chose `mice` throughout because it can
be fitted on the training rows and then applied to the test rows via `ignore`,
and because it gives five completed datasets. Those five agree on only
`r round(100 * agree["TUMOR_STAGE"])`% of the imputed stages, so the imputed
stage is uncertain, which is one reason I am not surprised that stage did not
survive the selection steps.

## 4. Principal components

PC1 captures `r round(100 * ve[2, 1], 1)`% and PC2 `r round(100 * ve[2, 2], 1)`%
of the variance in the scaled training features, so together
`r round(100 * ve[3, 2], 1)`%; the spread is flat, and it takes
`r which(ve[3, ] >= 0.8)[1]` components to reach 80%.
The largest PC1 loadings are `r paste(names(load_top(1, 5)), collapse = ", ")`
and the largest PC2 loadings are `r paste(names(load_top(2, 4)), collapse = ", ")`.
Reading them: PC1 mixes ER immunohistochemistry, integrative cluster 10 versus 4ER+,
grade, cellularity and TP53 in the directions you would expect of an aggressive
ER-negative, basal-like tumour, so I read it as a **tumour-biology axis**; PC2 is
dominated by stage, NPI, mastectomy and tumour size, a **disease-extent axis**.
Neither is a clinical quantity on its own, and the first two together hold only
`r round(100 * ve[3, 2], 1)`% of the variance, so PCA does not compress this data much.

* **Why scale first:** PCA chases variance, and variance depends on units. Age
  (years, SD about `r round(sd(Xc_tr$AGE_AT_DIAGNOSIS))`) would swamp a 0/1 mutation flag purely because of its
  scale, and the "components" would just be the largest-unit variables.
* **Why PCA before the split leaks:** the rotation is computed from the covariance
  of the data. If the test rows are in that calculation, the axes are chosen
  partly to describe the test patients, so projecting them is not a fair
  out-of-sample step. Here PC1 barely moves (cosine between the training-only and
  all-rows axis is `r round(cos1, 3)`) but PC2 rotates more (`r round(cos2, 3)`),
  so the axes really do depend on which rows were used, and fitting them on all
  rows would quietly make the test rows part of the definition of the features.
* **At the bedside?** No. PC1 is a weighted sum of `r length(keep_corr)` standardised variables,
  including genomic ones, each scaled with the *training* cohort's mean and SD.
  A clinician cannot compute it, cannot explain it to a patient, and a change in
  any input changes it in a way nobody can read off. A variable-level rule or a
  short score built from a handful of named inputs can be used; a PC score cannot.

## 5. What we owe the patients

Every row is somebody's illness and, in the cases here, often their death.
Being public and de-identified lowers the risk but does not remove the duty.

* **Do not try to re-identify anyone,** and do not link these rows to any other
  data source. Age at diagnosis, tumour size, cohort and a rare mutation can
  together narrow a patient to one person (the `CTNNA1` and `LDLRAP1` mutations
  are each found in a single patient).
* **Report in ways that cannot expose small groups:** I would not publish or
  circulate tables or plots of groups of one or two patients with a rare combination.
* **Use the data for the purpose it was shared for** (research on breast cancer),
  and describe what the model can and cannot do honestly. It was fitted on
  `r length(tr)` patients, one set of cohorts and an era with different
  treatments, and "Living" includes people with short follow-up, so it is not
  evidence about any individual's future.

**What I would refuse to do, even though nothing technically stops me:**
use this data (or a model built from it) to decide whether an *individual*
patient gets a treatment, an insurance product or access to care, or to try to
work out which real person a row belongs to. A prediction model that has not
been validated prospectively, with clinicians, on a different population should
not make or justify decisions about people.
